html:
An early Bronze Age culture of central Europe, from about 2300 to 1600 BCE, centred on Bohemia, central Germany and western Poland. It is named after a village near Prague, and the map shows it in 2000 BCE in central Germany.

The Únětice people made true bronze by alloying copper with tin, and their bronze axes, daggers and ring-shaped ingots spread widely. They grew rich on trade in metal from the ore mountains and in amber from the Baltic. Some chiefs were buried in great mounds with gold, as at Leubingen and Helmsdorf in central Germany.

The best known find of the culture is the Nebra sky disc, a bronze disc with a gold sun or full moon, crescent and stars, buried around 1600 BCE. It is often called the oldest known picture of the sky.

The culture grew out of the Bell Beaker and Corded Ware cultures and was followed by the Tumulus culture and then the Urnfield cultures. To the north lay the Nordic Bronze Age.
